room.vision: Choosing a real test area and one visual question starts our rover’s job: measure a room, make a supervised trip, and remember what it saw.

items.title: Build a Mobile Robot with ROS: Project Overview
items.creator: Josh Newans · Articulated Robotics
items.focus: Watch the opening overview for the three capabilities: remote driving, room mapping, and camera-based observations. Pick the one you most want to see your rover perform.
items.why: See how a small mobile robot combines the interests you are learning. This is a visual companion; our hardware choices and Jazzy instructions remain the build route.

items.title: RT-2: New model translates vision and language into action
items.creator: Google DeepMind
items.focus: Look at how the research connects camera observations, language, and robot actions. Name one future request you would like your rover to understand.
items.why: This shows a longer-term possibility for a physical assistant. Our first result is deliberately smaller: one room and one present/absent observation, with no manipulation or general language control.

fit.vision: Your measured fit coupon is the first step toward a mount that holds the rover’s camera and sensors steadily in place.

items.title: Modeling with 3D printing in mind
items.creator: Prusa Research
items.focus: Look at the orientation, support, and tolerance examples with your part in front of you. Identify the surface that must fit and the direction that carries its load.
items.why: You can see why a printable shape and a dependable robot part are different design problems. Use measured X1 Carbon coupons for your own dimensions.

model.vision: Your first model learns one question from your own images, ready for the rover to attach those observations to a time and capture pose.

items.title: But what is a Neural Network?
items.creator: Grant Sanderson · 3Blue1Brown
items.focus: Watch how an image becomes numbers and how weights change the output. Translate the digit example into our toy-present versus toy-absent question.
items.why: The animation gives a picture of what your training code changes. You can return to the experiment without mastering every equation in the series.

motion.vision: Commands, encoder feedback, and a tested stop turn the printed assembly into a mobile instrument for the room survey.

items.title: Build a Mobile Robot with ROS: Project Overview
items.creator: Josh Newans · Articulated Robotics
items.focus: Revisit the moving robot and trace one request from the operator to the wheels. Separate the job of driving from the jobs of sensing and mapping.
items.why: The assembled rover makes the purpose of each bench check visible. Use our selected controller and its documented checks when you wire your own robot.

sensing.vision: A stationary sensor check prepares the rover to place camera images, laser returns, and wheel motion together using known frames and times.

items.title: SLAM with slam_toolbox
items.creator: Josh Newans · Articulated Robotics
items.focus: Look at the laser observations and the robot display. Notice that the measurements need a position and orientation before they can form a coherent room.
items.why: Seeing the output gives the coordinate-frame work a purpose. The video is visual reinforcement; keep the course’s Jazzy configuration and actual sensor mounting measurements.

map.vision: Your room sketch and tape measurements become independent checks that make the robot’s map useful for understanding the room.

items.title: SLAM with slam_toolbox
items.creator: Josh Newans · Articulated Robotics
items.focus: Watch the grid map take shape as the robot observes the room. Look for revisiting an area, and compare that process with the reference spans you measured.
items.why: This is the visible result our mapping sessions work toward. Follow our recording, frame, and measurement checks rather than copying another robot’s configuration.

items.title: Episode 91 – Robot navigation on land and in water
items.creator: Robot Talk · Claire Asher with John Leonard
items.focus: Listen for the relationship between knowing where a robot is and building a map. Bring back one idea that helps explain your own room experiment.
items.why: John Leonard connects mapping and navigation to a wider field of real robots. This is optional listening, with no new software or prerequisite assignment.

navigation.vision: A checked map and dependable motion support a short requested trip, including knowing when the rover should stop or refuse the route.

items.title: Episode 91 – Robot navigation on land and in water
items.creator: Robot Talk · Claire Asher with John Leonard
items.focus: Listen for how navigation depends on observations and uncertainty, rather than a map alone. Relate that to a toy or chair moving after your survey.
items.why: The interview puts your small supervised route in the same family of questions as larger autonomous systems. It does not establish that this rover is ready for unattended household use.

memory.vision: Records of what an image showed, when it was captured, and the rover’s pose give us evidence for future questions about the room.

items.title: RT-2: New model translates vision and language into action
items.creator: Google DeepMind
items.focus: Inspect the examples connecting vision, language, and actions. Write down which observations and tested actions your own rover would need before answering one similar request.
items.why: This is research inspiration for the physical-assistant vision. Our current memory records and checked navigation are narrower capabilities; a language model does not supply missing measurements or robot skills.
